messages.subject: Loss of parameters in output file
parts:
Hi at all,

I have written a Stan-code to sample from a distribution, which has normally around 50 parameters. Because the function to sample from is pretty complex, I have written two codes expressing the function in two different ways. Both codes compile, run and provide output-files. I checked both codes with the built-in diagnostic tool: the error of the gradient lies for each parameter in both codes in the order of e-10 - e-07 (see attachments: *_diagnostics).

With the optimization tool I get for each code a log probability of around 70, but the highest log probability within the samples are mostly still negative (e.g. -18). That is not satisfying.

A much greater problem is the fact, that in the sample output file the 25. parameter is recorded only incompletely and the following parameters are totally lost. In the old fashioned style I printed the "lost" parameters during sampling on the screen and found that they definitely exist on run-time and are not NaN. Has somebody had the same problems with lost parameters? What could be the problem?

My next question concerns the two codes. Because the log likelihood function is pretty complex, the first code calculates the log likelihood in statement separated steps (see attachment: FRETnps_seq.stan). This means that the parameters are used already before the log probability is sampled/calculated. Is this even possible or in/correct?

Because I had doubts in this, I produced a second code in which the increment_log_prob-function explicitly contains/depends on the (transformed) parameters. But this leads to an ugly code (see attachment: FRETnps_one.stan).

Because I have no clue when the sampling step takes place, I'm still not sure which way is the correct one.

The next problem concerns the priors. In our case the number of priors can change in each scenario. That is why I have to read the number of position priors from the data sheet and declare an array of this length. Because each prior in the array has different bounds (but this is not supported by Stans modelling language) each one is bounded from 0 to 1. The individual prior borders are read from the data sheet and the priors are subsequently transformed in a new array. Is this way of dealing with highly divers priors correct or is there another better way?

Because all our priors are flat I just bounded them, what should lead to uniform priors!? Is this correct?

I appreciate any kind of help!

Best regards

Tobias

On Aug 8, 2014, at 11:14 AM, Tobias Eilert <tobias.e...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi at all,

> I have written a Stan-code to sample from a distribution, which has normally around 50 parameters. Because the function to sample from is pretty complex, I have written two codes expressing the function in two different ways. Both codes compile, run and provide output-files. I checked both codes with the built-in diagnostic tool: the error of the gradient lies for each parameter in both codes in the order of e-10 - e-07 (see attachments: *_diagnostics).
>
> With the optimization tool I get for each code a log probability of around 70, but the highest log probability within the samples are mostly still negative (e.g. -18). That is not satisfying.

Maybe not, but are you sure it's wrong? Often the optimized log density
is much higher than the density in the typical set. In very pathological
cases, such as sampling from beta(0.5,0.5), you'll find the optimizer
gets nearly infinite density before it halts, whereas the sampler will
be much better behaved.

> A much greater problem is the fact, that in the sample output file the 25. parameter is recorded only incompletely and the following parameters are totally lost. In the old fashioned style I printed the "lost" parameters during sampling on the screen and found that they definitely exist on run-time and are not NaN. Has somebody had the same problems with lost parameters? What could be the problem?

Nobody's reported losing parameters except in cases where the
program does not terminate normally. Did the program exit normally or
was there something that crashed it? Does the same thing happen
every time? If it happens every time (crash or no), could you let me know
which model and which data to run to reproduce the problem?

> My next question concerns the two codes. Because the log likelihood function is pretty complex, the first code calculates the log likelihood in statement separated steps (see attachment: FRETnps_seq.stan). This means that the parameters are used already before the log probability is sampled/calculated. Is this even possible or in/correct?

Every variable must be defined (not just declared) before it is used.
Parameters are automatically defined, as are data variables if you get
past init. All other variables (transformed data, transformed parameters,
local variables) must be defined before they are used.

> Because I had doubts in this, I produced a second code in which the increment_log_prob-function explicitly contains/depends on the (transformed) parameters. But this leads to an ugly code (see attachment: FRETnps_one.stan).
>
> Because I have no clue when the sampling step takes place, I'm still not sure which way is the correct one.

There's a pretty complete description in the manual in the part
on the language describing what happens in each block. See
chapter 18, "Execution of a Stan Program" for an overview, then
the rest of that part for complete (I hope!) details.

> The next problem concerns the priors. In our case the number of priors can change in each scenario. That is why I have to read the number of position priors from the data sheet and declare an array of this length. Because each prior in the array has different bounds (but this is not supported by Stans modelling language) each one is bounded from 0 to 1. The individual prior borders are read from the data sheet and the priors are subsequently transformed in a new array. Is this way of dealing with highly divers priors correct or is there another better way?

If you transform a variable then used the transformed variable on the
left side of the sampling ~, you need to include the log Jacobian determinants.
There are details in the manual chapter 13, "Reparameterizations & Change of Variables".
> Because all our priors are flat I just bounded them, what should lead to uniform priors!? Is this correct?

The default priors are uniform on the support of variables. If the
variables are bounded above and below, the priors will be proper.
Stan does not require proper priors, but does require proper posteriors.

- Bob

Hey Bob and Luc,

thanks for your replies!

It took a time to check out the problems I had/have. Regarding the loss of the parameters I changed now from cmdStan to RStan, what solved the problem. Now all parameters (and even when I add a few more) are wholly saved in the output-file. I don’t know what the problem with cmdStan is.

I searched the Stan users mailing list to get a complete explanation of the topic “Transformation”. But still I haven’t found problems, which are closely related to mine.

Suppose you have the following code, which is just an abstraction of mine to highlight my problem:
(I spared the data block and the declaration of the variables local to the model block for clarity! Please don’t mind implementation mistakes: It’s just an uncarefully shortened code to explain my question!!!)

parameters {


    // Positions

    vector<lower=0,upper=1>[3] pos[x];   

 

    // Polarangles

    real <lower=0,upper=pi()> phi[x];

    real <lower=0,upper=pi()> theta[x];


}

 

transformed parameters {

    

    // transformed position prior

    vector[3] transf_pos[x];

 

    // transition dipole moments

    vector[3] moment[x];

   

    for (j in 1:x){

 

        // linear transformation of position prior

        transf_pos[j] <- (prior_borders[1,j] - prior_borders[2,j]) .*

                          pos[j] + prior_borders[2,j];

 

        // non-linear transformation of polar angles

        moment[j,1] <- sin(theta[j]) * cos(phi[j]);

        moment[j,2] <- sin(theta[j]) * sin(phi[j]);

        moment[j,3] <- sqrt(1 – square(moment[j,1]) – square(moment[j,2]));                

 

    }

 

}

 

model {

   

    for (i in 1:y){

 

        // get indices of dyes

        dye1_ind <- dye_ind_of_meas[1,i];

        dye2_ind <- dye_ind_of_meas[2,i];

 

        // Log(Likelihood)-Calculation \\

           

            // Distance

            link_vec <- transf_pos[dye2_ind] - transf_pos[dye1_ind];

 

            dist <- sqrt(dot_self(link_vec));

           

            // <R^6>

                  // cThX

                  cThT <- dot_product(moment[dye1_ind], moment[dye2_ind]);

                  cTh1 <- dot_product(link_vec, moment[dye1_ind]) / dist;

                  cTh2 <- dot_product(link_vec, moment[dye2_ind]) / dist;

 

                  // <Kappa^2>

            Kappa2 <- square(cThT - 3.0 * cTh1 * cTh2)

 

            R_avg <- 1.5 * pow(R_iso[i],6) * kappa2;

               

            // FRET-Efficiency

            fret_eff <- 1.0 / (1.0 + pow(dist,6) / R_avg);

           

            // Log(Probability)-Function

            fret_eff ~ normal(fret_avg[i], fret_err[i]);

    }

 

}

 

If you don’t want to read my code I will explain again my problem literally:

Suppose you have 10 (two times 3 position- and 2 polarangle-parameters). They need to be transformed, because each position-prior has individual borders. Each position-parameter is transformed, meaning you get for each parameter one and just one transformed parameter! This means you would get a quadratic Jacobi-Matrix and you could calculate the determinant. In this case I don’t need to add the determinant of the Jacobi to the Log-Probability-function, because it is a linear transformation and it is only necessary to determine the Log-Probability-function up to constant in Stan.

Further the polarangle-parameters are changed to express the same vectors in Cartesian coordinates. Because these vectors have by definition the length one, only two parameters  (theta and phi) are transformed to three parameters moment[j,1], moment[j,2] and moment[j,3]. This means we need to construct a Jacobi-Matrix that is of type 3x2. Here the calculation of a determinant isn’t as trivial as above. Do we need then the generalized functional determinant (therefore the square of the gramian determinant) for R^n --> R^m transformation?

Now suppose we want to calculate the Log-Probability-function, but the function is so complex, that it is easier and better readable to calculate it from inside to outside. This is what happens in the model block in the above example.

The local variable fret_eff, which is normal distributed and defines the Log-Probability-function, depends on the distance (dist) between two positions (position-parameters) and on the so called averaged Förster Radius (R_avg), which is defined by various angles (cThX) between two moments (vector[3] moment) and the linking vector of two positions. This means I calculate at first the linking vector out of the two position vectors, its length as the distance and then the above mentioned various angles. The latter are used to calculate R_avg and finally we can define the sampling statement, which states that fret_eff is sampled from a normal distribution with variance and mean defined in the data block.

So from my understanding we need to adjust the Log-Probability-function with the Jacobi-determinant of the transformation, if we have a “Change of variables”, which means that the transformed parameters are sampled instead of the parameters! If this is correct, does it mean, that I have to build a huge Jacobi-Matrix from the variable fret_eff derived by all untransformed parameters (what would lead to an unsymmetric matrix, more exact to a row-vector) and calculate its gramian determinant to account for the curvature of the transformation?

 

To make my problem as clear as possible, here again in an example free way:

Is it allowed to split your function in several steps (outside of a sampling statement) and just sample the result of these split steps. If not, what is the correct way to handle this? If it is, are those steps considered as transformations? If they are considered as transformations (and we are dealing with “Change of variables”) how do you compute the determinant of an unsymmetric matrix (by gramian matrix?) in case of variable reduction during transformation?

I hope my question is clear enough and you can help me with this!

Thanks for your time!

Greetings

 Tobias

Hey Bob,

the problem is not that I just WANT to sample from a transformed parameter, but I HAVE to: First of all in each sampling scenario the number of position-priors differs, that means I need an array with flexible size! Further each position-prior has individual prior-borders (also changing in different scenarios), but in Stan you can not create an array where each field has different borders! So I have to create an array, where each field is bordered from 0 to 1 and transform them with the individual borders read in the data block. Because for the calculation of fret_eff the distance between the transformed position-priors is needed I can not sample from the first array of untransformed parameters!

Second of all the Log-Probability-function, if I write it directly depending on the transformed parameters (and not split into steps), is more than ugly and almost impossible to debug!

If you want a Stan-Code that reproduces in cmdStan the loss of parameters take one of those I've posted in my opening mail (e.g. FRETnps_seq.stan with data sheet FRETnps_data.data.R). Yesterday evening one possible reason came to my mind: I opened the data sheet with Excel. Maybe Excel is the problem...

Why should I want to sample fret_avg (= expectation of the fret_eff) which I get from the input? You're right with the vectorization! But before I think about the implementation I want to be sure that my code samples the correct posterior!!!

Thanks for your effort!

Greetings Tobias

> First of all in each sampling scenario the number of position-priors differs, that means I need an array with flexible size!

Stan doesn't have a ragged array data type, so the only way to
deal with this is with the ugly encoding demonstrated for LDA
in the manual.
> Further each position-prior has individual prior-borders (also changing in different scenarios), but in Stan you can not create an array where each field has different borders!
Correct.
> So I have to create an array, where each field is bordered from 0 to 1 and transform them with the individual borders read in the data block.

Correct. It doesn't matter where you start (other than for
efficiency) as long as you apply all the Jacobians necessary.

> Because for the calculation of fret_eff the distance between the transformed position-priors is needed I can not sample from the first array of untransformed parameters!
>
> Second of all the Log-Probability-function, if I write it directly depending on the transformed parameters (and not split into steps), is more than ugly and almost impossible to debug!
We don't have a solution for that.

> If you want a Stan-Code that reproduces in cmdStan the loss of parameters take one of those I've posted in my opening mail (e.g. FRETnps_seq.stan with data sheet FRETnps_data.data.R). Yesterday evening one possible reason came to my mind: I opened the data sheet with Excel. Maybe Excel is the problem...
Thanks.
> Why should I want to sample fret_avg (= expectation of the fret_eff) which I get from the input?

It's a different model. In a linear regression, you get y from the input
with coefficients beta and predictors beta, but you model it using a sampling statement.

y ~ normal(X * beta, sigma);

The normal is symmetric in the first two arguments, so technically this is the
same log probability increment:

X * beta ~ normal(y, sigma);
> You're right with the vectorization! But before I think about the implementation I want to be sure that my code samples the correct posterior!!!

Good idea.

- Bob
